performers: National Symphony Orchestra of London, Walter Goehr
intro: Walter Goehr conducts the National Symphony Orchestra of London in an orchestral version of Liszt’s Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 in C♯ minor, S. 244/2, recorded at Kingsway Hall in 1945. This is the opening disc side only.

sections.label: C · Orchestral phrases, louder
sections.mNote: The orchestral phrases return at full strength.

cues.title: Lassan, slow opening section
cues.text: Liszt begins with the Lassan, the rhapsody’s slow half. Grave phrases stand beside capricious short turns before the fast dance takes over. Liszt wrote the original for one pianist; in this recording Goehr directs an orchestra.
cues.evidence: The Lassan’s contrasting character is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2. The recording source identifies the orchestral performers but leaves the arranger unidentified: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PDP-CH_-_National_Symphony_Orchestra_of_London,_Walter_Goehr_-_Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2_in_C-sharp_minor,_S_244-2_-_Liszt_-_Decca-k1321-ar9230.flac.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Walter Goehr, Berlin and London
cues.text: Goehr studied with Schoenberg in Berlin and worked for Berlin Radio. As a Jewish musician he was forced to seek work outside Germany, and he moved to London to conduct for His Master’s Voice. His record labels sometimes called him George Walter.
cues.evidence: Goehr’s Berlin studies, emigration, recording work and alternative label names are documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Goehr.

cues.title: Sketchbook and publication, 1846–1851
cues.text: The rhapsody’s opening melody appears in Liszt’s sketchbook of 1846, written down after he heard it played. He published the piano work in 1851. Later, with Franz Doppler, he made an orchestral version in D minor.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard discusses the 1846 sketchbook, 1851 publication and Liszt–Doppler orchestral version: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9. Goehr’s orchestration is unidentified, so the historical arrangement is not assigned to this recording.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: Pianist whose playing drew orchestral sound from the keyboard, and who at the end of his life turned to sparse music at the piano.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces, and no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Liszt always counted Hungary as his homeland, though the languages he used most easily were German and French. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano, and Antonio Salieri taught him composition. In 1823 the family moved to Paris, where the Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. He continued his education with private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha.
